strengths: Introduces the first multiview, real-world benchmark (SceneDiff) with instance-level, per-object change annotations across substantially different viewpoints, filling a clear gap relative to prior benchmarks that either assume near-duplicate viewpoints or only provide per-view/semantic labels (Table 1 comparison is thorough and convincing).

The training-free SceneDiff method is well-motivated, combining off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction (π³), segmentation (SAM), and appearance (DINOv3) models via an asymmetric geometry-consistency score plus region-level appearance matching; the design choices (bidirectional visibility masks, asymmetric depth-difference rule, region-based rather than pixel-based matching) are sensible and clearly derived from failure modes of naive pixelwise comparison.

Extensive empirical evaluation: results on the new SceneDiff benchmark (per-view/per-scene/AP_type), on the existing two-view RC-3D benchmark, and on ChangeSim, with large margins over baselines (CYWS-3D, 3DGS-CD, a VLM+GroundingSAM pipeline).

Thorough ablations and diagnostic analysis in the supplement: contribution of each score term, comparison across geometry backbones (π³, VGGT, DUSt3R, Fast3R) and feature extractors (DINOv1/2/3), robustness to dynamic content, threshold sensitivity, and detailed failure-case analysis (cluttered repetitive scenes, low-overlap geometry failure, strong lighting) — this level of self-critical analysis is unusually strong and adds credibility.
Concrete downstream demonstration (robot tidying task) shows practical utility beyond benchmark numbers.

Clear annotation tool/protocol description and evaluation protocol (per-view, per-scene, per-scene-type AP) with illustrative figures, supporting reproducibility; commitment to release code, tool, and data.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains modest (e.g., 46.3 per-scene AP, 25.5 AP_type on SD-V; even lower on SD-K), and the paper's own failure analysis shows the method degrades substantially under cluttered/repetitive scenes, low view overlap, and strong lighting changes — the task is explicitly stated as unsolved, which somewhat limits the immediate impact/reliability of the method for real applications despite outperforming baselines.

The method is entirely training-free and built on several large pretrained foundation models (π³, SAM, DINOv3); this makes performance and reproducibility contingent on the continued availability/behavior of these external models, and the pipeline is fairly heavy (159s/pair, Table 6), which may limit practicality for real-time robotic use cases the paper motivates.

Baseline comparisons, while reasonably fair-minded (e.g., feeding regressed depth to CYWS-3D, adjusting 3DGS-CD sampling rate), could still be seen as somewhat favorable to the proposed pipeline since SceneDiff's own geometry/segmentation backbones are strictly stronger/more modern than what baselines were originally designed with; a more apples-to-apples ablation (e.g., baselines given the same π³ geometry) is only partially explored.

Dataset collection process (350 pairs from a guideline-driven, apparently small pool of contributors capturing casual videos) is not fully detailed in terms of number of annotators/contributors, potential biases in scene selection, or inter-annotator agreement for mask/label quality, which could affect diversity claims and annotation reliability.

The evaluation protocol (point-based matching with up to two tolerated extra detections per GT, dynamic entropy thresholding, oracle-comparable) is reasonable but somewhat permissive/complex, and its sensitivity to design choices (e.g., allowed FP tolerance) is not deeply analyzed relative to how it affects reported AP numbers.

The paper does not report variance/uncertainty (e.g., multiple runs, confidence intervals) given some stochasticity in thresholding and model outputs, nor statistical significance of the reported improvements over baselines.

strengths: Addresses a clear and under-served gap: existing change-detection benchmarks are limited to near-identical viewpoints or lack instance-level, per-scene (multi-view) annotations; SceneDiff is the first dataset offering instance-level object change annotations across video pairs with differing viewpoints, spanning 350 pairs / 1009 objects across diverse indoor/outdoor categories plus an egocentric cooking subset (HD-Epic).

The proposed training-free pipeline is a sensible and reasonably novel combination of existing foundation models (pi^3 for geometry, SAM for regions, DINOv3 for appearance), with a thoughtful asymmetric visibility-mask formulation to separate true change from viewpoint-induced occlusion, and a two-stage frame-level + object-level association scheme.

Experimental evaluation is extensive: results are reported on the new SceneDiff benchmark, the existing two-view RC-3D benchmark, and ChangeSim, with consistent and often large improvements over multiple baselines (CYWS-3D, 3DGS-CD, a VLM pipeline).

The supplementary material is unusually thorough, including ablations across different geometry backbones and feature extractors, threshold sensitivity studies, failure-case analyses (cluttered repetitive scenes, low-overlap geometry failures, strong lighting changes), robustness to dynamic content, running-time comparisons, and a qualitative robotic tidying demonstration.

The paper is candid about limitations (geometry-reliant failure modes, inherent ambiguity in swap-like changes, lack of fine-grained semantic/state change detection), which strengthens scientific credibility rather than overselling the contribution.

The annotation tool and dataset collection protocol are clearly documented, supporting reproducibility, and the evaluation protocol (per-view, per-scene, per-scene-type AP) is well specified and illustrated with visual walkthroughs.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons may be somewhat unfair: CYWS-3D and 3DGS-CD are not trained or adapted on SceneDiff's training/validation data, and the VLM baseline is a zero-shot GPT-4o + GroundingSAM pipeline; there is no learned baseline fine-tuned on SceneDiff to establish what a trained competitor could achieve, making the 'large margin' claims harder to contextualize.

Method novelty is primarily in orchestrating existing pretrained models (pi^3, SAM, DINOv3) rather than introducing new algorithmic or representational contributions; this is acceptable for a benchmark-centric paper but tempers the significance of the methodological contribution.

Absolute performance remains modest, especially on the harder SD-K (egocentric kitchen) subset (per-view AP 23.6 vs. 49.6 on SD-V, per-scene AP_type only 12.2), indicating the task is still far from solved and the method's robustness to real-world clutter/occlusion is limited, as also acknowledged by the authors' own failure-case analysis (cluttered repetitive scenes, low-overlap geometry failure).

The method depends on multiple hand-tuned hyperparameters (score weights lambda^g, lambda^f, lambda^r, merging/similarity/occlusion thresholds) that, while shown reasonably robust in validation-set ablations, were tuned on a small 50-pair validation split per subset and may not generalize cleanly to new domains.

Dataset collection appears to rely on a relatively small/distributed group of contributors following written guidelines, with no reported inter-annotator agreement or annotation quality verification beyond a review step, leaving data quality/consistency not fully quantified.

The point-based evaluation protocol (tolerating up to two unmatched predictions per ground truth) is somewhat permissive, and no sensitivity analysis is provided on how this tolerance affects the reported AP values relative to stricter matching criteria.

Inference cost (159.4s per sequence pair) is considerably higher than the CYWS-3D and VLM baselines, which may limit applicability in time-sensitive robotic or monitoring scenarios despite the demonstrated tidying-robot use case.

strengths: Introduces SceneDiff Benchmark, the first multiview object change detection dataset with instance-level, per-object annotations across genuinely different viewpoints (350 video pairs, 1009 annotated objects, 20 scene categories, indoor+outdoor), clearly filling a gap relative to prior benchmarks (RC-3D, 3DGS-CD, PASLCD, ChangeSim) that are smaller, single-object, or assume near-duplicate viewpoints.

Proposes a training-free method that composes pretrained 3D geometry (π3), segmentation (SAM), and appearance (DINOv3) models with an asymmetric depth-difference rule and region-level matching, avoiding the sim-to-real gap that afflicts end-to-end trained approaches and the render-quality bottleneck of Gaussian-splatting-based methods.

Strong, consistent empirical improvements over multiple baselines (CYWS-3D, 3DGS-CD, VLM+GroundingSAM) on both the new SceneDiff benchmark and the existing two-view RC-3D and ChangeSim benchmarks, with large relative margins reported.

Thorough ablations and analysis: comparison across geometry backbones (π3, VGGT, DUSt3R, FAST3R) and feature extractors (DINOv1/2/3), sensitivity to thresholds (τΔ, τmerge), robustness to dynamic content, and explicit failure-case analysis (cluttered repetitive-item scenes, low-overlap geometry failure, strong lighting changes) that honestly characterizes limitations rather than hiding them.

Practical downstream demonstration via a real robotic tidying application, plus a released annotation tool and detailed evaluation protocol (per-view, per-scene, per-scene-type AP) that supports reproducibility.

Clear, well-illustrated writing with extensive supplementary material (qualitative comparisons, evaluation-protocol visualization, timing, camera trajectories) that substantiates claims beyond the main text.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains modest, especially on the SD-K (kitchen/egocentric) subset (AP ~23.6/20.9, AP_type 12.2), indicating the method is far from solving the task in cluttered or egocentric scenarios; this is acknowledged but leaves practical readiness uncertain.

The method is a fairly heuristic composition of several pretrained modules with multiple hand-set hyperparameters (score weights λ^g/λ^f/λ^r, thresholds τocc, σgeo, σsim, σmerge); while threshold robustness is shown, the weighted score-fusion design itself is not ablated, so its sensitivity/generality is unclear.

Baseline comparisons (CYWS-3D, 3DGS-CD, VLM) are used off-the-shelf rather than retrained/fine-tuned on SceneDiff's provided train/val split, which could be seen as advantaging the proposed training-free approach that was itself tuned on the same validation set; a comparison against a baseline trained on SceneDiff would strengthen the claim of superiority.

Two acknowledged failure modes (dense repetitive-item scenes, low-overlap geometry reconstruction) are common in real applications (retail, warehouses, sparse-view robotics), somewhat limiting the scope of claimed generality despite being honestly reported.

Dataset collection process (guideline document, presumably lab/crowd-collected short clips) lacks details on annotator/recorder diversity, number of contributors, quality control, or consent/privacy handling beyond a brief 'avoid identity info' instruction, which affects assessment of dataset diversity and potential biases.

Methodological novelty is moderate: the core contribution is largely an effective engineering pipeline combining existing pretrained models (π3, SAM, DINOv3) with matching/aggregation heuristics rather than a new learning algorithm or theoretical insight, which is acceptable but should temper expectations of high novelty impact.

strengths: Introduces the first instance-level, multiview object change detection benchmark (SceneDiff) with 350 diverse real-world video pairs across 20 scene categories, indoor and outdoor, with dense object instance annotations — filling a clear gap relative to prior semantic/pixel-level or similar-viewpoint benchmarks (well summarized in Table 1).

Proposes a training-free method built by composing pretrained geometry (π³), segmentation (SAM), and semantic feature (DINOv3) models, enabling generalization across domains without retraining and the ability to improve as underlying foundation models advance.

Extensive empirical validation across four benchmarks (proposed SceneDiff, RC-3D, PASLCD, ChangeSim) with consistent, sizable improvements over strong and diverse baselines (pixel-level, box-level, 3DGS-based, and VLM-based), along with thorough ablations of geometry and feature backbones.

Commendable transparency: detailed failure-case analysis (cluttered/repetitive scenes, geometry reconstruction failure under low overlap, strong lighting changes), hyperparameter sensitivity studies, and robustness checks (dynamic content masking, alternative geometry models) that clarify the boundaries of applicability rather than only showcasing favorable results.

Practical downstream demonstration via a real robotic tidying application, plus a well-documented SAM2-based annotation tool that reduces annotation time, supporting reproducibility and future dataset extension.

Careful, well-justified adaptation of baseline methods (CYWS-2D/3D, 3DGS-CD, MV3DCD, VLM+SAM3) to the new benchmark, with supplementary analysis showing these adaptations do not unfairly disadvantage baselines.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains quite low even for the proposed method (e.g., obj/sc AP of 22.8/10.8, obj/im AP of 43.8/23.6 on the two SceneDiff subsets, and near-zero scores in the change-type-aware and cluttered-scene settings), indicating the task is far from solved; this is appropriately acknowledged but tempers the practical impact claims.

The method's core novelty is mainly in composing and scoring with existing pretrained components (3D reconstruction, SAM segmentation, DINOv3 features) rather than a new representation or learning approach; the individual technical modules (reprojection scoring, region matching, greedy association) are relatively standard.

The overall pipeline is heavily bottlenecked by the pretrained 3D geometry model — failure analysis shows that limited view overlap causes total reconstruction/detection failure, and different geometry backbones (e.g., VGGT) can invert static/moved object dynamics, raising concerns about robustness in less-controlled capture conditions.

Some evaluation design choices (thresholds for region merging/matching, aggregation into scene-level tracks, asymmetric geometry rule) are somewhat heuristic; although sensitivity analysis is provided and shows general stability, the chosen operating points and their generality to unseen domains are not deeply theoretically justified.

Dataset scale (350 pairs, ~1000 annotated objects) is modest by broader CV benchmark standards, and about 43% of the pairs (150) are drawn from an existing HD-Epic dataset rather than newly collected, somewhat limiting the novelty of the data diversity claim relative to the 200 self-collected pairs.

Only a single VLM baseline (Qwen2.5-VL + SAM3) is evaluated; comparisons against other recent multimodal/VLM-based reasoning approaches for change description would strengthen the claim of large relative improvement over 'existing approaches.'

strengths: Introduces a genuinely new and practically motivated task formulation: multiview object-level change detection across videos with differing camera trajectories, which is more realistic than prior near-identical-viewpoint settings.

SceneDiff Benchmark is reasonably large and diverse (350 sequence pairs, 50 scenes, 20 categories, indoor/outdoor, egocentric + manually captured), with a documented SAM2-based annotation tool and clear metric definitions (px/im IoU, obj/im AP, obj/sc AP) that address the practical ambiguity of counting objects vs. pixels.

The training-free method is a sensible, well-motivated pipeline (joint geometry regression + co-visibility frame pairing + asymmetric depth-difference scoring + DINOv3 appearance comparison + region-level matching + 3D-consistent instance association) that cleanly builds on strong pretrained components and is reported to generalize across domains without retraining.

Extensive empirical validation: comparisons against multiple baseline families (pairwise CYWS-2D/3D, 3DGS-based 3DGS-CD, VLM baseline), evaluation on three external benchmarks (RC-3D, PASLCD, ChangeSim) in addition to the new benchmark, thorough ablations on geometry/appearance backbones, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and a real robot tidying demonstration.

Commendable transparency about limitations and failure modes (cluttered/repetitive-item scenes, low-overlap geometry failures, strong lighting changes, ambiguous swaps between identical objects), with dedicated qualitative failure analysis in the supplement rather than only favorable cases.
Clear writing and figures; dataset, annotation tool, and code are promised to be released, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains quite low in several settings (e.g., obj/sc AP of only ~10.8 on SD-K and ~22.8 on SD-V), and the paper's own failure analysis documents that the method is unreliable in common scenarios (cluttered scenes with repetitive items, limited-overlap geometry, strong lighting), raising questions about real-world readiness despite the reported relative gains over weak baselines.

The method is largely an engineering integration of existing pretrained components (π³ for geometry, DINOv3 for features, SAM for segmentation) rather than a new learned model or theoretical contribution; novelty lies mainly in the scoring/aggregation pipeline, which is useful but incremental relative to the individual foundation models it depends on.

Baseline comparisons involve substantial re-engineering/adaptation of prior methods (e.g., converting CYWS-2D/3D boxes to masks via SAM, building bespoke region-matching rules for CYWS-3D, retraining 3DGS at higher frame rate than originally proposed, VLM scored via SAM3 since it lacks calibrated confidence) — while documented transparently, these adaptations introduce researcher degrees of freedom that could favor the proposed method and make an entirely fair comparison difficult to fully verify.

Dataset scale and collection process are modest: the Varied subset (200 pairs) was collected by only 7 people, and scene/category diversity, while reasonable, is still limited in absolute numbers relative to the breadth of applications claimed (robotics, warehouse inventory, disaster response); no discussion of annotation inter-rater reliability or potential annotator bias given manual point-prompt labeling.

The obj/sc AP metric design, including greedy matching, 0.5 IoU threshold, and confidence averaging across views, is somewhat ad hoc and not benchmarked against alternative formulations beyond the appendix's agnostic vs. change-type-aware comparison; sensitivity of conclusions to metric choices is only partially explored.

Heavy dependence on accurate camera pose/geometry regression (π³) is a core bottleneck acknowledged by the authors themselves (Sec. 7.7-7.8), and the system's behavior is shown to degrade or invert entirely under certain conditions (e.g., VGGT misidentifying static content as moved), suggesting the overall framework's robustness is closely tied to the idiosyncrasies of whichever geometry foundation model is used, which may limit the generality claimed in the abstract.

strengths: Introduces the first multiview object-change-detection benchmark (SceneDiff) with instance-level, dense annotations across 350 real-world video pairs spanning 20 diverse indoor/outdoor scene categories, filling a clear gap relative to prior pixel/semantic-level or similar-viewpoint benchmarks (well justified via the comparison table).

The training-free SceneDiff method is a sensible, well-motivated pipeline (joint geometry regression + asymmetric depth-based geometry cues + DINOv3 appearance cues + region-level matching + video-level object association) that cleverly avoids task-specific training data and thus is expected to improve as underlying foundation models improve.

Strong empirical results: large relative improvements over multiple baseline families (pixel-level, bounding-box, 3DGS-based, VLM) on the proposed benchmark, plus competitive/leading results on three additional established benchmarks (RC-3D, PASLCD, ChangeSim), indicating good generalization.

Extensive and honest analysis: ablations over geometry/feature backbones, hyperparameter sensitivity studies showing robustness to threshold choices, detailed failure-case analysis (cluttered repetitive scenes, low-overlap reconstruction failure, lighting changes), and clear discussion of limitations (ambiguous swaps, pose-estimation dependency, no semantic-state changes).

Practical utility demonstrated via a real robot tidying application, and a thoughtfully engineered SAM2-based annotation tool that substantially reduces annotation time, improving reproducibility and future extensibility of the dataset.

Supplementary material is unusually thorough (device/runtime reporting, camera trajectory visualizations, detailed baseline adaptation protocols for CYWS-2D/3D, 3DGS-CD, VLM, and additional dynamic-content robustness tests), which aids reproducibility and transparency about evaluation choices.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains quite low on the proposed benchmark (e.g., obj/sc AP of 22.8/10.6 under change-type-agnostic criteria, dropping further under change-type-aware evaluation), especially on the cluttered SD-K subset, indicating the task is far from solved; while acknowledged, this tempers the significance of the reported "53% relative improvement" framing.

The method's core reliance on off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction (π³) makes it fundamentally bottlenecked by geometry-model failures (low overlap, extreme lighting, dynamic content), and while these are discussed, they represent a structural rather than incidental limitation for real-world deployment.

The scene-level AP metric relies on several heuristic design choices (greedy matching, IoU aggregation across views, thresholding, region merging with hand-set weights/thresholds) that, despite the sensitivity analysis showing empirical robustness, add protocol complexity that could hinder independent reproduction or fair comparison by future work.

Dataset scale (350 pairs, 1009 objects) is modest in absolute object/scene count relative to some large-scale but less-tailored change-detection corpora, and the "Varied" subset was collected by only 7 people, which may limit scene/style diversity despite the stated category diversity.

Comparisons to some baselines (3DGS-CD, MV3DCD, CYWS-2D/3D) required non-trivial re-adaptation (mask conversion via SAM, occupancy grid removal, sampling-rate changes) which, though transparently documented, introduces some risk that baseline numbers are not fully representative of those methods' best-case performance.
Broader societal-impact/privacy considerations (e.g., use of egocentric HD-Epic videos, robotic tidying in real environments) are only minimally addressed in the main text.
